title: Telemedicine
description: Design a telemedicine platform — provider scheduling and booking, virtual waiting rooms, secure video visits, clinical notes and prescriptions, and HIPAA-grade security and auditing.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is a Telemedicine Platform?
blocks.text: A telemedicine platform (Teladoc, Practo, Doxy.me) lets patients book and attend medical appointments by video. It combines a booking system, a video call service, and a lightweight medical record: visit notes, prescriptions and documents. Because it handles health data, privacy, security and audit trails are core requirements, not extras.

items: Patients should be able to find providers by specialty and book an available time slot.
Patients should join a virtual waiting room and then a secure video visit with the provider.
Providers should be able to write visit notes and send prescriptions electronically.
Patients should be able to see their visit history, notes and prescriptions.
Lab orders and integrations with hospital EHR systems (mentioned briefly).

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Security and privacy: health data encrypted in transit and at rest, strict access control, full audit logging (HIPAA/GDPR).
A time slot can never be double-booked.
Video calls with low latency (< 300 ms) and good quality on weak connections.
High availability during clinic hours; a failed call must be recoverable quickly.
Massive scale — ~100k visits per day is a large platform.
**Appointment**: patient, provider, slot, status, video room ID.
**Clinical record**: visit notes, prescriptions, attachments — owned by the patient's chart.

blocks.text: Providers publish recurring availability, which is expanded into **slots**. Search filters providers by specialty and **licence jurisdiction** (a provider can only treat patients located where they're licensed). Booking atomically changes the slot from `open` to `booked` and creates the appointment.

At visit time, the patient opens the appointment and enters a **waiting room** (a presence channel over WebSocket); the provider sees who's waiting and admits them. Both sides get a short-lived **room token** and connect with **WebRTC**. For one-to-one calls, media flows peer-to-peer when possible, via a **TURN relay** when firewalls block it, or through an **SFU** for multi-party visits (interpreter, family member).

Providers write structured visit notes (SOAP format) during or after the call; notes are **signed and locked**, with later changes made as addenda. Prescriptions are sent to the patient's pharmacy through an **e-prescribing network** integration, with status tracked asynchronously.

The patient's chart aggregates visits, notes and prescriptions. Reads go through an **authorization layer** that checks the relationship (patient themselves, treating provider, delegated caregiver) and logs every access.
1) How do we prevent double booking?

approach.text: Check the slot is open, then create the appointment.

challenges.text: Two patients booking the last afternoon slot simultaneously both succeed.

approach.text: `UPDATE slots SET status = 'booked', patient = ? WHERE id = ? AND status = 'open'`, in the same transaction as inserting the appointment.

challenges.text: Patients filling in intake forms may lose the slot halfway through.

approach.text: When a patient starts booking, place a **hold** (`status = 'held'`, `heldUntil = now + 5 min`) with the conditional update; confirm it when intake completes. A sweeper (or a check on read) releases expired holds. Idempotency keys make retries safe, and a unique constraint on `(providerId, start)` for booked appointments backs it up.

challenges.text: Holds briefly hide slots from others, so keep the window short.

blocks.text: 2) How do we meet HIPAA-grade security?

Encrypt everything in transit (TLS, SRTP for media) and at rest with keys in a KMS. Use **least-privilege access** with role- and relationship-based checks on every record read, and write an **immutable audit log** of who accessed what and when. Keep health data in dedicated, segregated stores; never put it in logs, analytics or push notification text ("You have a new message" rather than the diagnosis). Sign Business Associate Agreements with any vendor (video, SMS) that touches health data.
Mention data residency: some countries require health data to stay in-country, so deploy regional stacks with region-pinned storage.
3) What happens when a call drops?

WebRTC connections monitor quality; clients reduce video resolution under poor bandwidth and fall back to **audio-only** before dropping. If the connection fails, both clients automatically rejoin the same room with their still-valid token. A **phone dial-in** fallback lets the visit continue by audio over the phone network.

quiz.question: How do we prevent two patients booking the same slot?
options: A conditional update from open/held to booked
quiz.explanation: The database guarantees only one booking succeeds.

quiz.question: Why use a TURN server in a video visit?
options: To relay media when firewalls block peer-to-peer connections
quiz.explanation: TURN keeps calls working on restrictive networks.

quiz.question: Why shouldn't push notifications include diagnoses?
options: Notification content can appear on lock screens and pass through third parties
quiz.explanation: Minimise exposure of protected health information.

quiz.question: Why are signed visit notes changed only through addenda?
options: To keep an accurate, auditable medical record
quiz.explanation: Medical records must show what was known and recorded at the time.
